## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will understand:

- The complete architecture of a Fortune 500 Kubernetes platform.
- How to map the tools we built (Prometheus, ArgoCD, Istio) to real-world business problems.
- The three types of Kubernetes interview questions and how to dominate them.
- The "STAR" method for behavioral incident scenarios.
- How to position yourself for six-figure Platform Engineering roles.

## Prerequisites

- Completion of Lessons 1 through 46.
- A mindset ready for production architecture and career strategy.

## Real-world Motivation

### From Lesson

The "Siloed Engineer" Problem: Many engineers know how to run `kubectl apply` or how to write a Deployment YAML. However, when an interviewer asks, "Walk me through how a request reaches a Pod, and how you would debug it if it failed," they freeze. They know the pieces, but they do not understand the system as a whole. Furthermore, they cannot translate technical knowledge into business value (for example, "I implemented Argo Rollouts to reduce deployment rollback time by 95%").

### From Lesson

Knowing Kubernetes is only half the battle. You must be able to architect systems that survive real-world traffic, and you must be able to articulate your value to non-technical hiring managers and highly technical interview panels. This capstone bridges the gap between "knowing Kubernetes" and "being a Kubernetes Engineer."

### Additional Production Knowledge

Every tool in this course is a business lever. In an interview, translate each skill into an outcome: Argo Rollouts reduces rollback time, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler lowers infrastructure cost, Network Policies shrink compliance scope, and GitOps with ArgoCD turns every deployment into a reversible git commit. Hiring managers fund outcomes, not YAML.

## Core Concepts

### From Lesson

- The Reconciliation Loop: A senior engineer sees Kubernetes as a collection of loops trying to make Actual State match Desired State.
- Defense in Depth: Security is not just RBAC. It is RBAC + Network Policies + Security Contexts + Kyverno admission controllers.
- Progressive Delivery: No human should ever type `kubectl apply` in production. Everything is automated via GitOps and safely rolled out using Argo Rollouts.
- The STAR Method: (Situation, Task, Action, Result) - the framework for answering behavioral interview questions.

## Architecture

### From Lesson (Architecture Overview)

If you walk into a company like Stripe or Shopify, this is what their platform looks like. Every component here is something you learned to build in this course.

```text
[ Developer Laptops / CI (GitHub Actions) ]
             |
             | Git Push: Code + Helm Chart
             v
[ Git Repository (Source of Truth) ]
             |
             +------------------------------+
             |                              |
             v                              v
[ ArgoCD (CD) ]                     [ Image Registry ]
  Reconciles Git -> Cluster           (Docker Images)
             |
             v
============== [ The Kubernetes Cluster ] ==============
[ Control Plane ]
    - API Server (Admission Webhooks / Kyverno)
    - etcd (Backed up via Velero)

[ Worker Nodes (Kubelet + Containerd + CNI/Cilium) ]
             |
             +--> [ Argo Rollouts ] (Progressive Delivery / Canary)
             +--> [ Ingress Controller (NGINX) ] (External Traffic L7)
             +--> [ Service Mesh (Istio Sidecars) ] (mTLS, Internal Traffic L7)
             +--> [ CoreDNS ] (Service Discovery)
             |
             +--> [ Application Pods ] (Probes, Requests/Limits, SecurityContext)
             +--> [ StatefulSets / Operators ] (Databases / RabbitMQ)
             |
             +--> [ Observability Stack ]
                   - Promtail (DaemonSet: ships logs to Loki)
                   - Node Exporter (DaemonSet: exposes metrics)
                   - Prometheus (Scrapes metrics, evaluates Alertmanager rules)
                   - Grafana (Visualizes Prometheus + Loki)
```

### Additional Production Knowledge

A platform team treats this diagram as a contract. The dashed lane between ArgoCD and the cluster is a pull-based reconcile loop, not a push. The mesh handles east-west (service-to-service) traffic with mTLS, while the Ingress handles north-south (external) traffic. Keeping those two planes separate is what lets you shift canary weight safely.

## ASCII Diagrams

### From Lesson (Visual Explanation - Mental Model)

Mental Model of a Senior Engineer: everything is a control loop.

```text
[ Git (Desired State) ]
      |
      v
[ ArgoCD Controller ] (Reconciles Cluster to Git)
[ HPA Controller ] (Reconciles Pod count to CPU metrics)
[ Argo Rollouts Controller ] (Reconciles traffic weights to error rates)
[ ReplicaSet Controller ] (Reconciles running Pod count)
```

### Additional Production Knowledge

Every controller is an instance of the same pattern: watch, diff, act, repeat. Pay attention inside the algorithm: a cache (or informer in client-go) holds a local copy of state so the controller does not hammer the API Server; rate limiting and retries prevent controller storms. Killing a reconciliation loop by abusing the API Server during an incident is a classic way to make things worse.

## Deep Explanation

### From Lesson

**1. Explain like I am 12**

Imagine a city. The Control Plane is the city government. The Worker Nodes are the factories. The Ingress is the highways. The Service Mesh is the secure courier service. The Observability stack is the traffic cameras and weather forecasters. To run the city, you do not just need to know how to build a road; you need to know how traffic flows, where the bottlenecks are, and how to respond when a bridge collapses.

**2. Explain like I am a junior engineer**

To pass a senior interview, stop thinking about individual resources (a Pod or a ConfigMap) and start thinking about systems. How does a code commit get to production? How do you know if the production app is healthy? How do you secure it? The architecture diagram above maps out that entire flow.

**3. Explain technically**

GitOps Flow: CI builds the image and updates the Git repo. ArgoCD detects the drift and applies it. Argo Rollouts intercepts the Deployment and turns it into a canary release, shifting 10% of traffic to the new version while querying Prometheus for error rates.

Data Path Flow: User -> Cloud LB -> NGINX Ingress -> Service IP (kube-proxy iptables DNAT) -> Pod IP (Istio sidecar intercepts for mTLS) -> Container.

Failure Domain: If a node dies, the Node Controller marks it `Unknown` after 40 seconds. The ReplicaSet controller notices missing Pods and schedules new ones on healthy nodes. The EndpointsController removes the dead Pod IPs from the Service, ensuring traffic routes only to healthy Pods.

**4. How Kubernetes implements it internally**

Kubernetes is an ecosystem of controllers. Everything you do - scheduling, networking, storage, deployments - is just a controller watching the API Server and taking action to align reality with your YAML.

## Terminology

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Platform Engineering | The discipline of building internal developer platforms. |
| SRE | Site Reliability Engineering. Focused on reliability, metrics, and incident response. |
| STAR Method | Situation, Task, Action, Result. A structured way to answer behavioral questions. |
| GitOps | Operating paradigm in which Git is the single source of truth. |

## How It Works Internally (The Interview Mindset)

### From Lesson

In an interview, you will be tested on three gates. You must pass all three to get an offer.

- **Core Knowledge**: Rapid-fire conceptual questions. For example, "What happens when you run `kubectl run`?"
- **Production Troubleshooting**: Scenario-based debugging. For example, "Users are getting 502s. Walk me through your steps."
- **Behavioral / Incident**: "Tell me about a time you handled an outage."

### Additional Production Knowledge

Interview panels are not looking for rote recall at the senior level; they look for structure. When given an open-ended debugging question, keep one funnel: symptoms -> surfaces -> data -> hypothesis -> action -> verify. It shows a disciplined engineering mindset, not just a vocabulary.

## Step-by-Step Workflow (Career Strategy)

### From Lesson

1. **Build a Portfolio**: Put your GitHub Actions pipeline, Helm charts, and ArgoCD configs in a public GitHub repo. This is your new resume.
2. **Get Certified**: Schedule the CKA exam within the next 3 months while this knowledge is fresh.
3. **Update LinkedIn**: Add "Kubernetes", "ArgoCD", "Prometheus", "Helm", and "GitOps" to your skills.
4. **Apply**: Target Platform Engineering and SRE roles. Use your portfolio to bypass HR filters.

## Lifecycle

### From Lesson

The lifecycle of your career transition:

- **Learning** (Done): You have completed this course.
- **Building**: You build your portfolio.
- **Certifying**: You pass the CKA.
- **Interviewing**: You apply and interview.
- **Operating**: You get the job and run production clusters.

## Hands-on (Final Capstone Assessment)

### From Lesson

Answer these 5 questions without looking at previous lessons. If you can answer them, you are ready for senior interviews.

1. A Pod is in `CrashLoopBackOff`. You run `kubectl logs <pod>` and see the app started fine. Why do you need to run `kubectl logs <pod> --previous`?
2. You deploy an HPA, but it shows `<unknown>/50%` for the target. What are the two most likely reasons?
3. You delete a PVC, but it stays in a `Terminating` status forever. Why is this happening, and how do you fix it?
4. How does ArgoCD detect and fix "Configuration Drift" if an engineer manually runs `kubectl edit`?
5. Why do we use a Headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) for a StatefulSet instead of a normal ClusterIP Service?

**Capstone Answer Key**

1. `kubectl logs` shows the current container's logs. Since it just restarted, those logs are fresh. `--previous` reads the logs of the crashed container instance that existed before the restart, which contains the actual stack trace or the `OOMKilled` event.
2. (a) The Metrics Server is not installed, or the HPA cannot reach it. (b) The Pod template is missing `resources.requests.cpu`, and the HPA needs a baseline to calculate percentages.
3. The PVC has a `kubernetes.io/pvc-protection` finalizer. It is waiting for a Pod that is actively using the PVC to terminate, OR the underlying PV has a Reclaim Policy of `Retain` and the cloud provider disk is stuck. You can fix it by removing the finalizer: `kubectl patch pvc <name> -p '{"metadata":{"finalizers":null}}'`.
4. ArgoCD continuously polls Git and compares it to the Live State in the cluster. If `selfHealing` is enabled, it detects the change as "Out of Sync" and sends a PATCH/PUT request to the API Server to overwrite the manual change back to the Git state.
5. A normal ClusterIP Service load-balances traffic randomly. Databases (StatefulSets) require specific peers to communicate (for example, `db-0` talking to `db-1`). A Headless Service does not load balance; it creates specific DNS A-records for each Pod IP, allowing direct routing to a specific database node.

## Commands

### Additional Production Knowledge

A short review of the commands that bind the capstone architecture together:

```bash
# Observe the cluster and its workloads
kubectl get nodes
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl describe pod <name>
kubectl logs <name> --previous

# GitOps: sync and diff with ArgoCD
argocd app get <app>
argocd app sync <app>
argocd app diff <app>

# Rollback and progressive delivery
kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout <name> --watch

# Insight: metrics, logs, and reconciliation
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods
kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
```

## YAML Explanation

### Additional Production Knowledge

Most of the YAML in the capstone diagram is the same you have already written. The single most important pattern is the interplay between Pod template metadata and controllers:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25-alpine
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 100m
            memory: 128Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 256Mi
```

- The `label` under `.spec.template.metadata` must match the `labelSelector` in the Deployment, and the Service uses the same labels so the EndpointsController wires traffic to the right Pods.
- The `requests` baseline feeds the HPA and enables percentage-based autoscaling; the `limits` enforce CPU and memory and prevent a noisy neighbor from starving a node.
- Deleting or changing the image in the template triggers a new ReplicaSet, which is exactly the hook Argo Rollouts and ArgoCD operate on for gradual and Git-driven delivery.

Adding a PodSecurityContext and SecurityContext is the counterpart: it runs the container as a non-root user with no extra capabilities, which is the baseline hardening already covered in Module 07.

## Troubleshooting (Interview Scenarios)

### From Lesson

**Scenario 1 - The 502 Bad Gateway**

Interviewer: "Users are getting 502 errors on your web app. Walk me through your debugging steps."

Ideal Answer:

1. Check the Ingress Controller logs to confirm the 502 is coming from NGINX, not the app.
2. Run `kubectl get endpoints <web-svc>`. If empty, the Service selector does not match Pod labels, or Pods are failing Readiness probes.
3. If Endpoints exist, check `kubectl describe pod` to ensure the container is Running.
4. If Running, exec into a utility Pod and `curl <pod-ip>:<containerPort>` to verify the app is actually listening on the port the Service targets.

**Scenario 2: The Node Failure**

Interviewer: "A node in your cluster goes offline. What happens to the Pods running on it?"

Ideal Answer:
- The node controller marks the node as `NotReady`. After a grace period (default 5 minutes), the node is evicted.
- The Pods on that node stay in `Terminating` state for a grace period (default 5 minutes).
- The ReplicaSet controller notices the Pods are gone and schedules new Pods on healthy nodes.
- The EndpointsController removes the dead Pod IPs from the Service, so traffic routes only to the new, healthy Pods.

### Additional Production Knowledge

For the 502 answer, always start from the cheapest data and work inward: load balancer/Ingress logs, then Service endpoints, then Pod status, then direct container probe. This "funnel" proves you debug from outside-in and never guess. For the node scenario, name the exact timers - `node-monitor-grace-period` (40s) and `pod-eviction-timeout` (5m) - to show command-level detail.

## Comparison Tables

### From Lesson

| Role | Focus | Key Tools |
|------|-------|-----------|
| DevOps Engineer | CI/CD pipelines, automation | Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Terraform |
| SRE | Reliability, metrics, incidents | Prometheus, Grafana, Argo Rollouts |
| Platform Engineer | Internal Developer Platform (IDP) | Kubernetes, ArgoCD, Helm, Crossplane |

## When to Use / When Not to Use

### From Lesson

Apply for Senior Roles **When**:

- You understood the concepts in this course and can build the architecture diagram above.
- You have 3+ years of general infrastructure or software experience.

Do **Not** apply for Senior Roles When:

- You are completely new to IT/Linux. Start with Junior DevOps or Cloud Support roles and work your way up.

## Performance and Security Considerations

### From Lesson

- **Performance**: In interviews, speed of thought matters. Use the mental models (for example, the "Troubleshooting Funnel") to structure your answers quickly.
- **Security**: Never share your company's proprietary Kubernetes manifests or code in an interview. Use open-source examples or sanitized versions.

## Real Company Examples

### From Lesson

**BlackRock**: At BlackRock, engineers do not have direct `kubectl` access to production clusters. They write YAML, open a Pull Request, and a CI pipeline runs tests. When the PR is merged, ArgoCD detects the new commit and deploys it. If an outage occurs, they can literally `git revert` the commit, and ArgoCD instantly rolls back the entire cluster state.

## Common Myths

### From Lesson

- Myth: "I need to know Go to be a Kubernetes Engineer." Fact: False. While Go is used to write Kubernetes operators, most Kubernetes engineering is YAML, Helm charts, and configuring infrastructure.
- Myth: "You need a CS degree." Fact: False. The best Platform Engineers often come from a systems administration or self-taught DevOps background.

## Production Notes

- A capstone project is only as strong as the write-up that explains the reasoning and trade-offs.
- Keep infrastructure-as-code, images, and reproduced logs with the project so reviewers can verify every claim.
- Production quality means documenting decisions, not just the happy path.

## Best Practices

- Prefer declarative manifests committed to Git over imperative `kubectl` commands.
- Add labels, resource requests and limits, probes, and least-privilege RBAC to every workload you present.
- Show your troubleshooting method, not just your answer.
- Reuse the manifests, diagrams, and cheat sheets from this repository as the foundation of the project.

## Common Mistakes

- Building a demo that works on a laptop but has no resource limits, no probes, and no documentation.
- Copying a whitepaper deployment without being able to explain any of its pieces.
- Avoiding the failure-mode discussion; interviewers are more interested in how you debug than in a flawless demo.

## Interview Questions

- Describe the architecture of the project you would present in this capstone.
- Walk through one incident you handled and exactly how you diagnosed it.
- How would you make this deployment safe for production, on a small budget?
- Which part of Kubernetes architecture is your strongest, and which is your weakest?

## Quiz

### From Lesson (True/False and Rapid Fire)

1. True/False: Taints repel Pods, while Tolerations allow Pods to bypass Taints. (Answer: True)
2. True/False: The Kubernetes Metrics Server stores historical data in etcd. (Answer: False - it is in-memory only.)
3. Rapid Fire: What port does etcd listen on? (2379)
4. Rapid Fire: What QoS class requires Requests == Limits? (Guaranteed)
5. Rapid Fire: What CNI uses eBPF to bypass iptables? (Cilium)
6. Rapid Fire: What command shows the history of a Helm release? (`helm history <name>`)

### Additional Production Knowledge

7. Which controller reconciles the running number of Pods toward the desired state? (The ReplicaSet controller.)
8. A Pod is scheduled but never starts; `kubectl describe pod` shows `Events` with `FailedScheduling`. Which workload binding the Pod to a node? (kube-scheduler, and it was blocked by scheduling constraints.)
9. True or False: A canary of 10% traffic, with no AnalysisTemplate, is safer than a blind rolling update. (Partially True: only if a metric or manual pause gates the promotion; without a gate it is still blind.)
10. Which component provides the initial metrics that the HPA uses for autoscaling? (kubelet/cAdvisor surfaced via the Metrics API, not etcd.)

## Revision Notes and Cheat Sheet

### One-Minute Revision

- **Architecture**: CI -> Git -> ArgoCD -> K8s -> Ingress -> Pod.
- **Debugging**: get -> describe -> logs -> endpoints.
- **Security**: RBAC + NetworkPolicy + SecurityContext + Kyverno.
- **Career**: Build a portfolio, get CKA, use the STAR method.

### Golden Rules of Kubernetes Engineering

- Declarative over Imperative: GitOps is king.
- Probes are Mandatory: Liveness and Readiness save lives.
- Least Privilege: Drop all capabilities, run as a non-root.
- Automate Everything: If you do it twice, script it. If you do it three times, automate it with an Operator.
- Observe Everything: Metrics tell you what, Logs tell you why.

### Cheat Sheet

| Concept | Tool / Command |
|---------|----------------|
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions + ArgoCD |
| Package Mgmt | Helm |
| Monitoring | Prometheus + Grafana |
| Logging | Loki + Promtail |
| Progressive Delivery | Argo Rollouts |
| Security | Kyverno + SecurityContext + NetworkPolicy |
| CKA Speed | `alias k=kubectl`, `export do='--dry-run=client -o yaml'` |

## Interview Preparation (The Ultimate Guide)

### Beginner Questions

Q: What is the difference between a Pod and a Container?

A: A container is a Linux process isolated by namespaces and cgroups. A Pod is a Kubernetes abstraction that wraps one or more containers, giving them a shared network IP and shared volumes.

### Intermediate Questions

Q: What happens when you run `kubectl run nginx --image=nginx`?

A:
1. kubectl sends a POST request to the API Server with a Pod manifest.
2. The API Server authenticates and authorizes the request (RBAC).
3. The request passes the admission controllers (for example, Kyverno).
4. The Pod is saved to etcd.
5. The kube-scheduler notices the Pod is Pending, filters nodes (taints, affinity) and scores them, then binds the Pod to a node.
6. The kubelet on that node notices the new Pod.
7. The kubelet calls the CRI (containerd) to pull the image and start the container via runc.
8. The kubelet reports the Pod status back to the API Server.

### Advanced / Scenario Questions

Q: You deployed a new version of your app. It passes Readiness probes, but users say the app is broken. How do you fix it, and how could Argo Rollouts have prevented it?

A: First, I revert immediately using `kubectl rollout undo`. To prevent it, I would use Argo Rollouts with a Canary strategy, sending 10% of traffic to the new version. An AnalysisTemplate would query Prometheus for 5xx error rates. If errors spiked, Argo would automatically abort and revert the traffic to the stable version.

## Scenario Questions

### Additional Production Knowledge

1. Q: A database StatefulSet reports that a single replica cannot connect to its quorum. The Service is a normal ClusterIP. What is the likely cable and the fix? A: The replica talks to peers by DNS name; a headless Service is required to expose per-Pod DNS A records so the replicas can address each other directly. Change the Service to `clusterIP: None`.
2. Q: You configure ArgoCD to sync a new image, but the rollout never leaves the Ingress. What do you check? A: Verify the Rollout reached a `pause` step or the AnalysisRun reported failures, then check the Rollout's status and the canary Service endpoints for the target Pods.
3. Q: A rollout to a new image is progressing, but users report slow responses. Where do you look? A: Follow the troubleshooting funnel: Ingress logs, then the target Service endpoints, then the Pod status and container Health probes.

## Mini Project

### From Lesson

Project: The Portfolio Repository.

1. Create a new public GitHub repository.
2. Add your Helm chart from Lesson 30.
3. Add your GitHub Actions workflow from Lesson 32.
4. Add a README.md explaining the architecture (use the diagram from this lesson).
5. Put the link to this repository on your LinkedIn profile and resume.

## Homework and Additional Reading

### From Lesson

- **Homework**: Schedule your CKA exam. Having a date on the calendar forces you to review and practice.
- **Additional Reading**: The Kubernetes Book, Site Reliability Engineering (Google), ArgoCD Documentation.

## References

- [Kubernetes Documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/)
- [Argo Rollouts Documentation](https://argoproj.github.io/argo-rollouts/)
- [The Kubernetes Book](https://www.amazon.com/Kubernetes-Book-Nigel-Poulton-books/dp/1538987359/)
- [Site Reliability Engineering (Google)](https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/)

## Standalone Diagrams

For a larger, reusable view of the concepts above, see these ASCII diagrams:

- [`14-cka-workflow.txt`](../../diagrams/14-cka-workflow.txt)  — 14 Cka Workflow

## Related Lessons

- [Lesson 24 - Helm Deep Dive (Writing Production Charts)](../09-packaging/lesson-30-helm-deep-dive-writing-production-charts.md) - the charts you put into the portfolio project.
- [Lesson 32 - CI/CD Pipelines (GitHub Actions and ArgoCD)](../10-gitops/lesson-32-cicd-pipelines-github-actions-and-argocd.md) - the CI/CD you reference in the portfolio.
- [Lesson 43 - Progressive Delivery (Argo Rollouts)](../12-production/lesson-40-progressive-delivery-argo-rollouts.md) - the rollouts that make the canary safe.

## Coming Next

Congratulations. You have reached the end of the course. You started by learning what a Linux namespace is, and you ended by designing a multi-cluster, GitOps-driven, auto-scaling, self-healing, zero-trust platform with progressive delivery and centralized observability. You are no longer someone who only "uses Kubernetes." You understand how it works under the hood, how to break it, and how to fix it under pressure.

Keep building the portfolio, schedule your CKA, and go earn the role. This repository is now your reference, your interview guide, and your proof of skill.

# File: architecture.md

---
title: Interview - Architecture
module: 02 Architecture
status: Complete
tags: [interview, architecture, control-plane, nodes, kubelet, scheduler]
---

# Interview - Architecture

## Beginner

**Q: What does the API Server do?**

A: It is the front door to the cluster. It authenticates and authorizes requests, runs admission control, and persists objects to etcd. It is the only component that talks directly to etcd.

**Q: What does the scheduler do?**

A: It watches for Pods with no node assigned and binds them to nodes by filtering (capacity, taints, affinity) then scoring candidates.

**Q: What is etcd, and what does it store?**

A: etcd is the cluster's backing key-value store. It stores every API object (Pods, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, CRDs) plus lease/heartbeat data. The API server is the only client that talks to it, and it is typically deployed as a 3- or 5-member cluster using Raft for consistency.

**Q: What is the kubelet responsible for?**

A: It is the node agent. It registers and watches its node, receives Pod specs (via the API server or as static manifests), creates Pods through the CRI, runs probes, mounts volumes, reports node status and resources, and enforces the node's resource allocation.

## Intermediate

**Q: What happens when you type `kubectl run nginx --image=nginx`?**

A: kubectl POSTs a Pod manifest to the API Server; the API Server authenticates and authorizes (RBAC), runs admission controllers, and stores the Pod in etcd. The scheduler sees the Pending Pod, picks a node, and binds it. The kubelet on that node sees the bound Pod, asks the CRI (containerd) to pull the image and start the container via runc, then reports status back.

**Q: A node goes offline. What happens to its Pods?**

A: The node controller marks the node NotReady after the grace period (default 40s for `node-monitor-grace-period`). Pods on it are evicted after `pod-eviction-timeout` (default 5m). The ReplicaSet controller schedules replacement Pods on healthy nodes, and the EndpointsController removes the dead Pod IPs from Services.

**Q: What is the role of kube-proxy?**

A: It maintains network rules (iptables/ipvs) that implement Services, translating ClusterIP:port into backing Pod IPs (DNAT).

## Advanced

**Q: How does etcd elect a leader and what happens when the leader fails?**

A: etcd uses the Raft consensus protocol. Members vote, and a candidate wins when it collects a majority. All writes go through the current leader, which replicates them to a quorum of members before acknowledging. If the leader fails or a member loses contact, a new election starts and the cluster must again make a quorum (majority is enough; a non-voting minority is fine as long as more than half remain reachable). A lost leader does not stop reads for the surviving majority, but anything requiring a write (e.g., a new Pod) blocks until quorum is reestablished.

**Q: What is the quorum math for a 3-member and a 5-member etcd?**

A: Quorum = floor(N/2) + 1. For 3 members, quorum is 2, so you can lose 1 member only. For 5 members, quorum is 3 and you can lose 2. That is why an odd number matters: with 2 members you can lose 0 and a split-brain becomes two minorities; with 4 members you still do not gain in failure tolerance (you lose one) while the latency cost goes up. In practice run 3 for most clusters, 5 for large control planes.

**Q: What is the difference between a `list` and a `watch`, and what does `resourceVersion` mean?**

A: `list` fetches a full snapshot of current objects with a `resourceVersion`. A `watch` reuses that `resourceVersion` to stream subsequent change events (Added/Modified/Deleted). Since a watch can drop events (restarts, errors), clients use a versioned watch and the API server returns a `410 Gone` if a resourceVersion is too old, telling the client to re-list and start a fresh watch. Controllers and informers do exactly this.

**Q: What is a static Pod and a mirror Pod?**

A: A static Pod is defined in a directory (default `/etc/kubernetes/manifests`) and read by the kubelet directly, without going through the API server. The kubelet creates a reflected, read-only copy of it in the API, called a mirror Pod (annotated `kubernetes.io/config.mirror`). You cannot `kubectl delete` a static Pod through the normal path; you remove the manifest file and the kubelet removes both. Static pods have no owner references, so they are never evicted by the kubelet's node lifecycle.

**Q: In which order do admission controllers run?**

A: A request is authenticated and authorized first, then runs the admission chain, and within it all mutating webhooks run in the configured `admissionregistration.k8s.io` order, then the object is validated (schema + ValidatingAdmissionWebhooks) in order too. Mutating webhooks may run sequentially, and the API server re-runs defaulting after mutation. Since a webhook can change the object others see, each admission controller defines a deterministic order; that order is surfaced in the API server's dynamic admission DAG (the `order` field on `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration`/`MutatingWebhookConfiguration`). Mutating is *always* completed before validating.

**Q: What are the two phases of the scheduler, and what is an extender?**

A: In the Filter phase, the scheduler removes nodes that cannot host the Pod (unsatisfied `nodeSelector`, taints/tolerations, affinity, `unsatisfied affinity`, or resource insufficiency — this is the Feasibility/Predicates step). In the Score phase it ranks the remaining nodes (balanced resource allocation, image locality, rack/zone balance). You can attach a scheduler extender (webhook) either after Filter to prune more or after Score to bias the ranking; note the scheduler's HTTP API lets an extender filter and prioritize but the actual binding is still done by the scheduler core.

**Q: What is the difference between `controller-manager` and `kube-scheduler`?**

A: Both run as controllers on the control plane. The kube-scheduler only assigns Pods to nodes (it produces a new `NodeName` and posts a Binding). Everything else — observing the desired vs current state and acting — is done by the kube-controller-manager: it runs many controllers behind it (ReplicaSetController, DeploymentController, NodeController / lifecycle and eviction, EndpointsController, ServiceAccount/Token controllers, etc.), each watching its own resources. Most also use a leader-election lease so that replicated instances pick a single active leader.

**Q: What happens on a graceful node shutdown and what are `PreStop` / `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`?**

A: When a node shuts down, the kubelet (with the `GracefulNodeShutdown` feature) identifies terminal pods and marks them with `shutdown-grace-period` priority, and for each, runs `preStop` hooks and waits for `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30s) before the container runtime sends SIGKILL; the kubelet also drains workloads that can be stopped. `preStop` gives the process a chance to unregister, flush, and clean up before SIGTERM crosses. The timer applies per-container and is not global; a long-running graceful drain therefore needs the pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` raised.

**Q: What are the PodSecurityContext fields and what could go wrong with them?**

A: The `securityContext` (or `PodSecurityContext`) on a Pod covers `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup`, `fsGroup`, `runAsNonRoot`, `seccompProfile`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, and `readOnlyRootFilesystem`. A classic trap is setting `runAsNonRoot` to true on a Pod whose image runs as root anyway — the runtime lists it as not non-root and fails to start. `fsGroup` creates a group change on the volume and is irrelevant to processes; people confuse it for an actual user. `readOnlyRootFilesystem` alone does nothing to stop writes to the /dev tmpfs or an overlay.

**Q: What happens when a webhook refuses a request during admission?**

A: The request is rejected atomically: the API server does not create or modify the object, the error is returned to the caller, and any mutation the webhook already applied is discarded alongside the failed attempt. That is why webhooks must be idempotent and deterministic, and why a Pod stuck in Pending with a failed create is a diagnostic clue — check `kubectl get events` for the `FailedCreate` reason and fix or remove the webhook, then retry.

**Q: What is API Priority and Fairness (APF)?**

A: APF replaced the coarse `--max-requests-in-flight` / `--max-mutating-requests-in-flight` flags with per-flow schemas and queues. Requests are classified into priority levels (e.g., `system`, `leader-election`, `workload-high`, `catch-all`) and served from queues with a bounded number of "seats"; a single loud client cannot starve others. `kubectl get --raw /debug/api_priority_and_fairness/dump_priority_levels` shows the current queue state while debugging throttling.

**Q: What are the leader-elected singletons on the control plane?**

A: kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler, and cloud-controller-manager each run leader-elected: one holds a Lease (`coordination.k8s.io`) and works, the others wait and take over on failure. They give failure tolerance, not throughput. The only component you horizontally scale for request handling is the stateless API server.

**Q: "The scheduler only needs CPU and memory to place a Pod." True or False?**

A: False. It also checks taints/tolerations, node and pod affinity, `nodeSelector`, topology spread constraints, inter-pod affinity, and the kubelet's actual allocatable vs capacity. Even a seemingly tiny pod is filtered out if the kubelet's reserved system resources (`--system-reserved` and `--kube-reserved`) shrink the allocatable below the request.

**Q: "A taint with `NoExecute` evicts a Pod immediately."**

A: No. `NoExecute` tells the scheduler not to place new Pods and starts the event clock on existing ones, but those Pods are only evicted after `tolerationSeconds` expires (checked every cycle). For `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready:NoExecute` the default is 300 seconds. So a node that is NotReady does not immediately kill its Pods; the kubelet-node cadence plus `pod-eviction-timeout` (5m) for the node controller drives the actual removal.

**Q: "When the API server dies, the scheduler cannot run."**

A: False. The scheduler is stateless: it keeps no local state of its own, and on reconnection it re-lists from the current `resourceVersion` and continues. The trap is thinking the scheduler stores the "best node" and that the API death loses work; what actually happens is the control-plane binaries block on their watch. Restart the API server and the watch re-establishes.

**Q: "Every node has a `kubelet`; a single kubelet can be pointed at two control planes."**

A: Trap. A kubelet registers exactly one Node object on one API server at a time, using its `--kubeconfig`. Pointing it at a second API server is not a supported trick; a multi-cluster setup needs separate agent processes. This trap shows up when people try to sync storage or launch static manifests on a "shared" node.

**Q: "A `PreStop` hook always runs before `SIGTERM`."**

A: Yes, but only when Kubernetes can do it: the hook group (hook + terminationGracePeriodSeconds) runs before the container receives SIGTERM. The trap: PreStop does not guarantee *completion* before SIGTERM — it competes with the grace period and SIGKILL can end it mid-flight. So plan for the process to be able to handle being killed even after a short hook.

**Q: "A `PodDisruptionBudget` protects a Deployment from losing replicas."**

A: Half true. A PDB does not protect against node loss (`node.kubernetes.io/not-ready` taint eviction is *not* a PDB event), against the ReplicaSet deleting a bad pod, or against a forced eviction. It only constrains voluntary disruptions like `drain` and `scale-down`. During a crash or an OOM the PDB is invisible.

**Q: "A scheduler with one replica and a controller-manager with three replicas is fine."**

A: Yes — this is intended. Only one scheduler runs (`--leader-elect`), and the controllers-manager elects one leader; extra replicas are idle hot standby. The trap: the scheduler and controller are both `leader-elected`, so scaling a control-plane to many replicas does not parallelize scheduling the way horizontal scaling of the API server does.

## Scenario

**Q: The control plane is down and etcd lost quorum. What do you do?**

A: Restore etcd from the latest backup to one member, let it form quorum again, then restart the remaining control plane components. Keep etcd backups current and test restores regularly.

**Q: A Node reports `NodeNotReady` but the kubelet process is running. What do you check first?**

A: For a node, look at `kubectl describe node` conditions first, then on the node check `journalctl -u kubelet`, the container runtime socket (`/var/run/containerd/containerd.sock`) health, and the CNI/network plugin. A hanging overlay or disk can keep kubelet running while Pods cannot start, so also check `/var/lib/kubelet` disk space and mount health.

**Q: You `kubectl cordon` a node, but the ReplicaSet still matches. Why do the Pods stay Running?**

A: `cordon` only marks the node unschedulable; it does not evict existing Pods. Eviction requires the `node.kubernetes.io/not-ready` taint's `tolerationSeconds` to expire (default 300s) or a `kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets`, and a `PodDisruptionBudget` (`minAvailable`/`maxUnavailable`) can still block eviction. Check `kubectl get pdb --all-namespaces` and the node's taints; if a PDB blocks you, approve or temporarily disable it, then drain.

**Q: You restart a Controller (informer) and it "missed" an event. Should you worry?**

A: No, that is the design. Informers `list` and then `watch` from a `resourceVersion`; if a watch is broken the API server returns `410 Gone` and the informer re-lists from the new `resourceVersion`. What you lose is only the affected period, whose state is re-read by the next list. A deeper problem is if you write code that relies on the initial list only and does not keep watching.

## Commands and Quick Reference

| Command | Why you run it |
| --- | --- |
| `kubectl get --raw /readyz?verbose` | Confirm the API server's own health checks (etcd connectivity, authorizer, controller); `?verbose` lists each check individually. |
| `kubectl get events --field-selector reason=FailedScheduling` | See exactly why a Pod was not placed on a candidate node. |
| `kubectl describe node NODE` | Get capacity, allocatable, taints, and the pod list on a single node. |
| `kubectl taint nodes node key=value:NoSchedule` | Temporarily make a node unschedulable for maintenance without deleting it. |
| `kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets` | Safely evict pods before maintenance; add `--delete-emptydir-data` when emptied volumes are acceptable. |
| `kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}'` | Extract the Ready condition of every node in one expression for a prompt. |
| `kubectl debug node/NODE --image=busybox` | Run a privileged pod on a node to inspect its host network, filesystem, or cgroup state. |
| `kubectl get --raw /metrics` and `kubectl top nodes` | Inspect kubelet and cAdvisor metrics when a node is slow or spiking. |
| `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector spec.nodeName=NODE` | See everything a given node is currently running. |
| `crictl ps -a` / `crictl logs` | Inspect containers from the CRI side, below the kubelet's abstraction. |
| `etcdctl endpoint health` / `etcdctl member list` | Verify etcd quorum and member health before any etcd surgery. |
| `kubectl get pdb --all-namespaces` | Find the PDB that is silently blocking a drain/eviction. |

## Related

# File: capstone.md

---
title: Interview - Capstone and Certifications
module: 14 Certifications
status: Complete
tags: [interview, capstone, cka, career, STAR]
---

# Interview - Capstone and Certifications

## The Three Interview Gates

1. **Core knowledge** - rapid-fire conceptual questions (e.g., `kubectl run` flow).
2. **Production troubleshooting** - scenario debugging (e.g., 502s).
3. **Behavioral / incident** - "Tell me about a time you handled production." Use the STAR method.

## STAR Method

**Situation, Task, Action, Result.** Structure incidents that way: set the context, state your task, explain the specific action, and quantify the result (e.g., "reduced time to detect by 80%").

## Certification Comparison

| Attribute | CKA | CKAD | CKS |
|-----------|-----|------|-----|
| Focus | Cluster administration and operations | Application design, build, and deployment | Security of clusters and containerized workloads |
| Core role | Cluster admin: etcd backup/restore, kubeadm, node management, RBAC, upgrades | App developer: Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, storage | Security specialist: hardening, admission, network security |
| Number of questions | 15-20 performance-based tasks | 15-20 performance-based tasks | 15-20 performance-based tasks |
| Duration | 2 hours | 2 hours | 2 hours |
| Passing score | 66% | 66% | 67% |
| Exam environment | Remote-proctored, browser terminal with real clusters, kubectl only | Same environment, per-task clusters | Same environment; requires a valid CKA first |
| Allowed resources | kubectl + official Kubernetes docs only (kubernetes.io/docs, kubernetes.io/blog and subdomains, helm.sh/docs, Gateway API docs); no arbitrary internet access | Same doc set as CKA | Same doc set plus security-focused docs |
| Distinct skill | Cluster admin: scheduling, taints, upgrades, TLS, troubleshooting | App dev: rollout patterns, probes, metrics, configurability | Security: hardening, audit logging, runtime security, network policies |
| Recertification | Certificate valid for 2 years (3 years if earned before 1 Apr 2024); renew by passing again | Certificate valid for 2 years (3 years if earned before 1 Apr 2024) | Certificate valid for 2 years; renew by passing |

## Exam-Taking Strategy

### Time Apportioning

- Skim every question first; solve the easy ones early so the time budget adds up.
- Budget roughly 13-18 minutes per high-value scenario and never spend more than 30 minutes on a single task. Flag long ones and return if time allows.
- Revisit flagged questions only after every easy task is fully answered.

### Know the Exam Environment

- The exam gives multiple clusters; each question targets a different one. Start every question with `kubectl config current-context`, then `kubectl config use-context <name>`.
- Generate templates with `kubectl run|create --dry-run=client -o yaml > manifest.yaml`, then apply.
- Small changes: `kubectl patch` or `kubectl edit`. Use `kubectl apply --force` only when a conflicting resource must be recreated.

### Reusable Snippets / Cheatsheet

- Set aliases and functions in the exam bashrc at the start; they save 10-15 minutes across 15+ tasks.

```bash
alias k='kubectl'
alias kg='kubectl get'
alias kd='kubectl describe'
alias kn='kubectl config current-context'
alias krf='kubectl apply --force -f'
```

The shell persists between questions, so the aliases defined once save minutes on every task. Keep each question's generated YAML in the home directory so you can patch and re-apply fast.

### Do NOT Recreate the Cluster

- Rebuilds cost minutes; never tear down the whole cluster for one broken object.
- Recover instead: `kubectl delete <object> --force --grace-period=0` then apply a fixed manifest, or `kubectl delete pod --force` to let Deployments reconcile.

### Verify With kubectl

- `kubectl get all -n <ns>`, `kubectl describe <res>`, and `kubectl explain <res>` are your primary diagnostics inside the exam.

## Interview Strategy / Do and Don't

**Do:**

- Admit when you don't know, then reason out loud.
- Show a debugging approach; walk through logical step-by-step isolation (events, describe, logs, taints, CNI).
- Ask clarifying questions before jumping to a fix.
- Mention tradeoffs explicitly (e.g., "that trades latency for resilience").
- Tie every technical answer to a production consequence ("this change would restart the Pod and drop in-flight requests").
- Use the STAR method for behavioral answers.

**Don't:**

- Answer with memorized jargon without explaining it.
- Dismiss tool versions (state which version you last used).
- Ignore business impact (RTO/RPO, cost, user disruption).
- Downplay security ("it's a test cluster, no one will attack it").

## Recap Checklist / 24-Hour Final Review

The night before the interview or exam, run this loop rapidly:

- **Rapid-fire recall:** ports (etcd 2379, API server 6443, kubelet 10250), NodePort range 30000-32767, probe types, Service types, QoS classes, taint/toleration syntax, PV/PVC flow, RBAC verb set.
- **One scenario demo:** re-run a single debugging drill end to end - "Pod CrashLoopBackOff" -> `kubectl describe pod` -> `kubectl logs --previous` -> fix the root cause -> verify with `kubectl get all` and `curl`.
- **STAR story ready:** rehearse one real incident out loud with a measured outcome (time to detect, requests recovered).
- **Review the environment:** if it is CKA/CKAD day, walk through the bashrc snippet above once more so the setup is instant.

## Quick Facts to Recall

| Fact | Value |
|------|-------|
| etcd port | 2379 |
| API Server | 6443 |
| Kubelet port | 10250 |
| NodePort range | 30000-32767 |
| node-monitor-grace-period | 40s (NotReady) |
| pod-eviction-timeout | 5m |
| QoS class | Guaranteed = requests == limits |
| CNI with eBPF | Cilium |
| Helm history command | `helm history <name>` |

## Portfolio Blueprint

- Public repo: your Helm charts, GitHub Actions pipeline, ArgoCD/GitOps config.
- A README explaining the architecture diagram (CI -> Git -> ArgoCD -> K8s -> Ingress -> Pod).
- Sanitized examples: no proprietary manifests or secrets.
- Link it on LinkedIn and your resume. Target Platform Engineering and SRE roles.

## Common myths

- You must know Go? No: controllers are Go, but most Kubernetes engineering is YAML, Helm, and infrastructure.
- You need a CS degree? No. Systems and self-taught DevOps backgrounds are common.

## Related

- [Revision - Certifications](../revision/certifications.md)
- [Module 14 - Certifications Index](../docs/14-certifications/README.md)
- [Lesson 43 - CKA Exam Masterclass](../docs/14-certifications/lesson-43-cka-exam-masterclass.md)
- [Lesson 44 - Cluster Architecture and the Kubeconfig File](../docs/14-certifications/lesson-44-cluster-architecture-and-the-kubeconfig-file.md)
- [Lesson 45 - etcd Backup and Restore](../docs/14-certifications/lesson-45-etcd-backup-and-restore.md)
- [Lesson 46 - The Capstone (Architecture, Career and Interview Mastery)](../docs/14-certifications/lesson-46-the-capstone-architecture-career-and-interview-mastery.md)

# File: configuration.md

---
title: Interview - Configuration
module: 06 Configuration
status: Complete
tags: [interview, configuration, configmap, secret, resources, quota]
---

# Interview - Configuration

## Beginner

**Q: What is a ConfigMap?**

A: A resource for storing non-secret configuration as key/value pairs, injected into Pods as environment variables or mounted files.

**Q: What is the difference between ConfigMap and Secret?**

A: Secrets are intended for sensitive data and are base64-encoded in `data` (with plain `stringData` in manifests). Both are used the same way, but Secrets should be encrypted at rest and managed carefully.

**Q: What is the `immutable` field on ConfigMaps and Secrets?**

A: It makes the resource read-only after creation. You cannot modify or delete a ConfigMap or Secret marked immutable; you must delete and recreate it. This gives the kubelet a guarantee that the mounted data never changes, which improves performance because the kubelet does not need to watch for updates.

**Q: What are resource requests and limits in simple terms?**

A: Requests are the amount of CPU or memory the container is guaranteed and reserved for scheduling. Limits are the maximum the container may use; exceeding a memory limit kills the container (OOMKilled), while exceeding a CPU limit throttles it.

## Intermediate

**Q: How do you inject a Secret into a Pod?**

A: As env vars via `secretKeyRef` or `envFrom`, or mounted as a volume. The token path `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount` is the ServiceAccount token.

**Q: What happens when you change a ConfigMap?**

A: Mounted volumes update after a short delay. Env vars are set at Pod start and do not update until the Pod is recreated.

**Q: `envFrom` vs individual `valueFrom` references - what is the difference?**

A: `envFrom` injects every key of a ConfigMap or Secret into the environment in one shot, which is convenient but conflicts can arise if keys collide or are invalid. Individual `valueFrom` entries map one specific key to one env var name, giving explicit control and renaming. Prefer individual references when keys are not valid identifiers for env vars, or when you need to select only part of the data.

**Q: What is the difference between `data` and `stringData` in a Secret?**

A: `data` holds values that are base64-encoded. `stringData` holds plain text values that the API server encodes at write time; it is never written back to the stored object, so you should not expect to read `stringData` back. Use `data` for programmatic consumers and `stringData` for readability in GitOps manifests.

**Q: What are the common Secret types?**

A: `Opaque` (arbitrary key/value), `kubernetes.io/tls` (for `tls.crt` and `tls.key`), `kubernetes.io/dockercfg` / `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` (registry credentials), `kubernetes.io/basic-auth`, and the service account token type. The type is metadata: it helps controllers and tooling interpret the fields correctly.

**Q: What is a ResourceQuota and what does it enforce?**

A: A ResourceQuota constrains total resource usage in a namespace: aggregate requests and limits across all Pods (e.g. `requests.cpu`, `limits.memory`), plus counts for objects like Pods, Services, PVCs. It is a namespace-level policy creating errors when the sum would exceed the quota. It does not set per-Pod defaults.

**Q: What is a LimitRange, and how does it differ from a ResourceQuota?**

A: A LimitRange applies per-object policies within a namespace: min/max for a single Pod or container, and default requests/limits when a Pod does not set them. A ResourceQuota governs the total across the namespace. They operate at different levels: a LimitRange can add default requests that a ResourceQuota then counts against.

**Q: What is the default environment for a Pod if requests and limits are not set?**

A: If no LimitRange exists, a Pod defaults to no requests and no limits, classified `BestEffort`. It may be scheduled anywhere and can use all node resources, but under memory pressure it is evicted first.

## Advanced

**Q: What are resource units for CPU and memory, and how are they written?**

A: CPU is measured in cores, written as integer or milli-core (`1`, `500m`, `0.5`). Memory uses the binary units `Ki`, `Mi`, `Gi`, `Ti` (2^10 scale) and the decimal SI units `k`, `M`, `G` (10^3 scale); they differ, `1Gi` is 1024 Mi but `1G` is 1000 M. Confusing `Mi` with `M` is a classic source of quota and capacity mismatch surprises.

**Q: What is the `envFrom` vs `env` interplay for Secret and ConfigMap keys?**

A: `envFrom` imports every key as a container env var name. If a key is not a valid identifier (e.g. contains `-`), the invalid keys are skipped silently. With `env` you control the exact mapping through `secretKeyRef`/`configMapKeyRef`. When both set the same env var name, the last entry in the list wins. Mounting the data as files has no such name restrictions, since filenames can hold arbitrary characters.

**Q: Why is a value you changed in a mounted ConfigMap sometimes still old, and how does the kubelet sync period cause it?**

A: Mounted files refresh when the kubelet syncs the Pod from its local cache, driven by the kubelet sync period (default 1 minute) plus a watch or volume refresh. This is not instantaneous, so a change to the ConfigMap can lag up to ~1 minute. Env vars do not update at all until the Pod is recreated.

**Q: How are Pods ordered for eviction when the node hits memory pressure?**

A: Kubelet evicts based on usage above capacity/requests. Priority order is effectively: BestEffort pods are evicted first, then Burstable pods over their requests, then Guaranteed pods last (and even Guaranteed can be evicted when it exceeds its limits). You can tune with `--eviction-hard`. Requests and limits are what sort pods into the QoS buckets.

**Q: What is the exact rule for a Guaranteed QoS Pod?**

A: Both requests and limits must be set for both CPU and memory on every container, and they must be equal (request == limit) for each resource on each container. If a request is omitted, the kubelet defaults it to the limit, so equality can be inferred. Burstable = at least one request or limit set and requests != limits for some resource. A Pod of any QoS class can still be killed when it exceeds a memory limit it set (cgroup OOM), independent of eviction order.

**Q: What is the relationship between a memory limit and OOMKill, and what about CPU limits?**

A: A memory limit creates a cgroup limit; if the container exceeds it the kernel OOM-killer kills a process in that cgroup (`OOMKilled` while other Pods stay healthy). CPU limits are throttling: the cgroup is allowed to use only the limited CPUs, so the process continues but only slower. A container with a CPU limit has no similar kill and pause; the limit is enforced by throttling.

**Q: What happens when a container requests more than the node can offer, or when limits are unset?**

A: If requests exceed what any node can satisfy, the scheduler leaves the Pod `Pending` (Unschedulable), not OOMKilled. If limits are unset but requests are, the container can burst beyond its request and consume spare node capacity until other workloads are evicted; this is why large `requests` without matching limits still keeps the Pod safely schedulable but allows noisy-neighbor spikes.

**Q: Actually, what is the difference between requests and limits on scheduling?**

A: Requests participate in scheduling: the sum of requests across pods must fit on the node, and the scheduler uses them to find a fit. Limits are only enforced after placement, by throttling (CPU) or the cgroup (memory). Increasing limits without increasing requests may place too many pods on a node (oversubscription) and then let them throttle or get killed.

**Q: What is the interplay between `resources.requests` and nodes with allocatable capacity?**

A: Kubelet reports `Allocatable`, which is `capacity` minus reserved system resources; requests are what the scheduler uses to fit Pods onto a node. Setting a request larger than allocatable leaves the node unable to admit the Pod. Requests affect scheduling and eviction, limits affect throttling and OOM - a key distinction to remember.

**Q: What are the differences between `immutable: true` and a normal ConfigMap for running workloads?**

A: With an immutable ConfigMap you trade flexibility for safety: no hot updates, no accidental drift, and the kubelet can skip watch and hash overhead. Any rollout that removes/renames the CM fails with a NotFound until a new CM is created and referenced. Use immutability for long-running config that changes rarely.

**Q: What is "encryption at rest" and what supports it in Kubernetes?**

A: Encryption at rest protects data inside etcd: the kube-apiserver encrypts objects as they are written, using the `EncryptionConfiguration` and an `--encryption-provider-config` file. Providers include `aesgcm`, `aescbc` (legacy), `identity` (no-op), and `kms` (an envelope with a KMS or cloud manager). Secrets, ConfigMaps and other object types are included. This is separate from encryption in transit (TLS): a Secret fetched by `kubectl get secret -o yaml` is base64-encoded, which is *not* encryption, and the value is only protected at rest if etcd encryption (or KMS) is enabled.

**Q: How are ServiceAccount tokens provided to Pods and when is a Secret used?**

A: The kubelet places a projected ServiceAccount token at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token` - a JWT minted by the API server. Modern clusters use a projected, short-lived, bound token; the `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` Secret type is the legacy fallback. Additional secrets can be created and mounted by referencing them in the Pod spec.

**Q: What are best practices for secret rotation and injection?**

A: Prefer volume mounts over env vars so updates are picked up; avoid env-var injection for anything sensitive because any process that can read `/proc/<pid>/environ` (including with `hostPID`) can see the values. Note that trailing whitespace in file-mounted values is stripped. Rotation typically means recreating the Secret and letting the kubelet refresh mounted files, or forcing a rollout.

## Gotchas

**Q: True or False: Base64 encoding makes a Secret encrypted on the wire and at rest.**

A: False. Base64 is encoding, not encryption or obfuscation. Anyone with access to the Secret object (and to etcd when encryption at rest is off) can decode it trivially. Real protection comes from RBAC, encryption at rest, and reducing secret exposure.

**Q: True or False: A Secret can be updated while a Pod mounts it and the container immediately picks up the new values.**

A: False for env vars; only mounted files are refreshed, and only after the kubelet sync. Env-var injection is fixed at Pod creation. If you need live updates, mount the Secret as a volume and re-read it, and account for the kubelet sync period.

**Q: True or False: A Pod with a memory limit can be OOMKilled by the kernel even if the node has free memory.**

A: True, and the common wrong answer is "the node must be out of memory first". A memory limit creates a cgroup boundary for the container; usage at the limit triggers an OOM kill inside that cgroup even when other node memory is idle. The QoS class does not protect against hitting your own container limit.

**Q: True or False: BestEffort pods have no requests and no limits, so they can stick on a node forever.**

A: False on two fronts. BestEffort pods have no requests or limits, but that means they hold no reservation and consume every resource they touch; the kubelet evicts them first under node memory pressure. "Sticks forever" is the opposite of reality - they are cleared first, not last.

**Q: True or False: Adding a CPU limit without a memory limit makes the Pod QoS Guaranteed.**

A: False. Guaranteed requires requests equal to limits for both CPU and memory on every container. A CPU-only limit (or any request != limit) makes the Pod Burstable. Guaranteed is an all-or-nothing classification.

**Q: True or False: A ResourceQuota and a LimitRange do the same job.**

A: False. ResourceQuota caps totals in a namespace (aggregate requests, limits, and object counts). LimitRange sets min/max and defaults for individual Pods and containers. They operate at different levels and you often need both.

**Q: Common wrong answer: "Setting a memory limit too low can crash the host node."**

A: The kernel OOM kill hits the container's cgroup first, not the host. Node-level memory pressure is governed by the sum of requests versus node capacity and the eviction thresholds, not by any single container's low limit.

## Commands and Quick Reference

| Task | Command |
|------|---------|
| List ConfigMaps | `kubectl get configmaps` |
| Detail a ConfigMap | `kubectl describe configmap <name>` |
| Create a ConfigMap from key/value | `kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=key=value` |
| Create a ConfigMap from file | `kubectl create configmap <name> --from-file=<path>` |
| List Secrets | `kubectl get secrets` |
| Detail a Secret | `kubectl describe secret <name>` |
| Create a generic Secret | `kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-literal=key=value` |
| Create a TLS Secret | `kubectl create secret tls <name> --cert=cert.crt --key=key.key` |
| Show encoded Secret values | `kubectl get secret <name> -o yaml` |
| List ResourceQuotas | `kubectl get resourcequota` |
| List LimitRanges | `kubectl get limitrange` |
| List Pod resource usage | `kubectl top pod` |
| Check a node's allocatable | `kubectl describe node <node>` |

## Scenario

**Q: Your app is killed with OOMKilled. How do you fix it?**

A: Check memory usage with `kubectl top pod`, raise memory `limits` and `requests` (and the app's heap limits), or investigate a memory leak. Never set a memory limit lower than the app needs.

**Q: You roll out a new ConfigMap version and the app still reads the old config for minutes.**

A: If the app reads it via env vars, the change never applies until Pod recreation, so that explains it. If mounted, the kubelet refreshes files on its sync period (default ~1 minute) and the app must re-read them; many apps cache config, so a restart or a sidecar to watch the config may be needed. Best answer: mount the config, make the app watch the filesystem, or roll the Deployment.

**Q: A new ResourceQuota is applied and a Pod immediately fails with a "exceeded quota" error.**

A: Quota is enforced at admission: the Pod creation is rejected with an `exceeded quota` message. Check `kubectl get resourcequota -o yaml` for `used` vs `hard`, and compare the new Pod's requests/limits against the remaining headroom. A LimitRange can also reject the Pod if the request is outside the allowed min/max, or silently add defaults that push the total over the quota. Each Pod often needs explicit `resources` set.

**Q: One container uses all machine memory. What is the usual reason?**

A: Often the container has no requests and limits (BestEffort) and the app leaks, so over time it devours all node RAM and the kubelet starts evicting other Pods. Set realistic requests and limits and add monitoring. If you set a generous memory limit but forgot requests, the scheduler still only reserves the requests - the limit alone does not protect the node from overcommit.

## Related

- [Revision - Configuration](../revision/configuration.md)
- [Lesson 21 - Resource Management and the OOMKiller (Requests vs Limits)](../docs/06-configuration/lesson-21-resource-requests-limits-and-quotas.md)
